channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: GLP-1s Are a Bigger Business Than AI
gist: Ro's CEO argues the core flaw of US healthcare is that the patient isn't the customer, and that GLP-1s (now out-earning consumer AI) prove cash-pay DTC cuts out PBMs/insurers, lowers prices and raises manufacturer profits; he predicts 50%+ of Americans on GLP-1s within 10-15 years. He details Ro's growth from $250M to $3B+ run rate after a 2022 refounding, AI-driven care, and stigma-busting celebrity marketing.

themes.theme: GLP-1s as a mass-market drug class

insights.claim: Ro's CEO predicts 50%+ of Americans will be on some form of GLP-1 within 10-15 years, up from an estimated 10-15% today, using statins (40-50 million US users) as a comp for a far more effective, broader-label drug.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Implies a multi-decade volume runway for Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk well beyond current obesity-penetration models.

insights.claim: Bottoms-up, ~75% of the US population is overweight or obese and thus clinically eligible for GLP-1s; top-down, only 10-12% of Americans are metabolically healthy, so even the healthy may take them prophylactically for inflammation or geroprotection.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: TAM framing that supports bullish long-run GLP-1 volume assumptions; tolerability improvements are the gating factor.

insights.claim: GLP-1 labels have expanded in about four years from diabetes only to obesity, heart disease, sleep apnea, liver disease and kidney disease, with trials in neurodegeneration, pain, addiction, mental health and cancer prevention, putting them upstream of the leading causes of death.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Label expansion keeps widening the addressable market; watch neuro/addiction readouts as next catalysts.

insights.claim: GLP-1 revenue now exceeds consumer AI revenue, and roughly twice as many individuals pay for GLP-1s as pay for AI, which the guest frames as a weakness in the AI narrative: insufficient day-to-day consumer impact.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Consumer willingness to pay is currently stronger for GLP-1s than AI subscriptions; relevant for comparing consumer-spend durability.
insights.quote: individuals pay for GLP1s twice the number of people uh pay for GLP1s that then pay for AI

insights.claim: The guest compares Novo and Lilly to OpenAI and Anthropic: many companies had the same generational GLP-1 or AI tailwind but few rode it to the same extent; distribution execution separates winners.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: In tailwind sectors, back the clear share leader rather than assuming the tide lifts all participants.

insights.claim: Stigma around staying on weight-loss drugs indefinitely is irrational: nobody expects cholesterol or birth-control benefits to persist after stopping, so chronic GLP-1 use should be treated like any other ongoing medication.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Chronic-use normalization supports recurring-revenue (subscription) economics for GLP-1 makers and distributors.

insights.claim: Oral and next-generation GLP-1s plus better tolerability are expected to broaden uptake, while affordability remains the main open constraint on mass adoption.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Watch oral-formulation launches and cash-price cuts as adoption accelerants.

insights.claim: The central flaw of US healthcare is that the patient is not the customer; whoever controls the flow of money at point of purchase (employers, insurers) is the stakeholder everyone builds around.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Businesses that let patients pay directly (cash pay) can capture share where incentives are misaligned.
insights.quote: whoever controls the flow of money at the point of purchase that's the customer

insights.claim: When GLP-1s went direct-to-consumer cash pay, PBMs and insurers were cut out and prices fell from ~$1,300 list to $149 while manufacturers still made more money, because volume growth far outstripped price declines (visible in Lilly's earnings).
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: DTC channels are structurally negative for PBMs and accretive to drugmakers' gross profit despite lower list prices.
insights.quote: prices go from $1,300 to $149 and the people making the drugs are making more money

insights.claim: Branded drugs historically rise 6-8% every year until the patent cliff; direct-to-consumer cash pay eliminates the list-to-net spread (e.g. $1,300 list drugs netting $300-400 behind the scenes).
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Erosion of list-to-net games threatens PBM rebate economics.

insights.claim: PBMs are described as the 'appendix' of healthcare: they once served a purpose nobody remembers, and software can do what they historically did.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for PBM-heavy business models (rebate capture) as DTC pharma channels scale.
insights.quote: PBMs to me are like they are like the appendex of the healthare system

insights.claim: Healthcare works best where it is cash pay with the patient as customer: LASIK and cosmetic surgery show costs falling and quality and convenience rising, and GLP-1 DTC is now the largest example.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Look for categories migrating to cash pay as deflationary, consumer-brand opportunities.

insights.claim: Repatha's price fell from about $600 a month to about $200 (60-70% lower) when it went direct-to-consumer, mirroring the GLP-1 pattern.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: DTC price resets may spread to other branded cardiometabolic drugs.

insights.claim: Hospital price-transparency laws are 'lipstick on a pig'; the guest favors giving individuals a rollover healthcare spending account (e.g. ~$20k of an employer's $20-25k per-person spend) plus catastrophic insurance so providers must publish prices to win customers.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Policy drift toward HSA-style consumer-controlled dollars would favor DTC providers over employer-plan intermediaries.
insights.quote: No industry could survive with its prices not being public

insights.claim: GLP-1 demand is rewiring the system, questioning why employers decide coverage when employers care about many employees over a shorter horizon than an individual's lifetime; industries get rewired when large numbers of buyers care about one thing for a sustained period.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Employer-sponsored coverage of high-cost chronic drugs is under pressure; DTC cash channels absorb the overflow.

insights.claim: Drug inventors should capture more of the margin than access aggregators; the guest likens Ro to Costco, earning thin product margins but a durable membership-based business.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Expect pharma to keep pricing power; distributors' value lies in aggregation and membership economics, not drug margin.

themes.theme: Ro's platform, growth and competitive edge

insights.claim: Ro grew from about a $250 million run rate to over $3 billion in roughly four years, about 100% year-over-year growth, while shrinking headcount from ~600 to ~400.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: A private DTC health platform at $3B+ run rate with high revenue per employee is a likely future IPO candidate and a key GLP-1 channel.
insights.quote: we've gone from about a $250 million run rate to over a $3 billion run rate

insights.claim: Ro claims to be the leading US provider of GLP-1s, signing up two to five times as many patients daily as competitors per credit card data.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: DTC GLP-1 distribution is consolidating around a leader; relevant to competitors such as pharma-direct platforms.

insights.claim: Ro is integrated with both Novo and Lilly, offers cash pay plus free AI-driven insurance checks (used by over 1% of the US population), and multi-month subscriptions saving patients $600-$1,800 a year.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Multi-manufacturer integration positions Ro as a neutral marketplace pharma wants to compete within.

insights.claim: Ro vertically built its own EMR, CLIA/CAP-accredited lab, pharmacy software and provider network in a condition-agnostic way, which let it scale fast when GLP-1s arrived; it frames itself as a care and treatment distribution platform rather than a condition-specific business.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Condition-agnostic infrastructure gives optionality to add new drug categories as they emerge.

insights.claim: Ro's business spans four categories: cardiometabolic (largest, fastest growing via GLP-1s), sexual health, dermatology and fertility.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Revenue concentration in GLP-1s ties Ro's trajectory to GLP-1 pricing and supply.

insights.claim: The CEO argues the only durable differentiation is continued innovation; feature checklists are temporary.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Assess consumer health platforms by innovation cadence rather than static feature parity.

insights.claim: Every patient message to Ro is routed through an LLM, side effects are structured into tasks assigned to providers with SLAs, yielding a 24/7 sub-30-minute side-effect response time.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Shows how AI ops lowers cost to serve while improving quality metrics in telehealth.

themes.theme: AI, data and the coming patient revolution

insights.claim: Three tailwinds drive a 'patient revolution': human biology coming online (labs, genetics, wearables), AI making 'what used to require a specialist now requires a prompt', and new treatments that radically shift health outcomes.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Consumer health platforms combining data, AI and drug distribution are positioned to commoditize concierge care.
insights.quote: what used to require a specialist now requires a prompt

insights.claim: Investors paying $100K a year for concierge doctors now ping Claude for $20 a month and find it better, signaling AI disruption of premium physician services.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Pressure on high-priced concierge models; tailwind for AI-native care delivery.
insights.quote: they ping Claude for 20 bucks a month and it's way better

insights.claim: The goal is a whole new form of healthcare for the price of Netflix by turning concierge care from a service into a commodity product.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Signals a low-price, high-volume subscription strategy for consumer healthcare.
insights.quote: a whole new form of healthcare for the price of Netflix

insights.claim: AI excels where there is structured data, verifiable rewards and tight feedback loops; medicine has unstructured data and slow feedback (death, heart disease), so the opportunity is shortening discovery cycles.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Back AI-bio efforts that create structured, fast-feedback data loops.

insights.claim: The PCSK9 story took ~26 years from the 2000 Dallas Heart Study (faulty PCSK9 gene carriers with LDL 30-40 had 85-90% lower heart disease risk) through Amgen's Repatha to Merck's oral PCSK9 approved this year; the guest argues AI should compress such timelines.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Oral PCSK9 could mass-market LDL lowering; cardiovascular prevention is a large emerging category.

insights.claim: Ro is mining its GLP-1 patient base with genetic, wearable, lab and self-reported data to explain response variation (e.g. why men lose less than women, why some lose 35% of body weight and others 5%).
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Proprietary outcomes data at scale could become a defensible asset for personalized prescribing.

insights.claim: US healthcare is better than credited at acute care (higher cancer and heart attack/stroke survival than OECD peers, fewer and shorter hospital stays) but has higher prices and far higher administrative burden; stagnant life expectancy reflects 'fast clock' deaths (guns, cars, overdoses) and chronic-disease 'slow clock' rather than care quality.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Administrative cost and chronic disease, not acute care, are where value creation lies.

insights.claim: Healthcare spending as a share of GDP should be as high as possible (even 50-70%) because via Jevons paradox another healthy year is the only good without diminishing marginal returns; the problem is rising cost per unit, not total spend.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Healthcare remains a secular growth sector; deflationary unit-cost models can expand the market.
insights.quote: I think it should be as high as possible. 50 70

insights.claim: US healthcare spend went from 9% to 18% of GDP, UK from 6% to 12%, Germany from 9% to 12%; the US is a preview of where other countries are heading, not an anomaly.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Global healthcare spend growth supports international expansion of US health models.

insights.claim: US health dollars split roughly 30-35% hospitals, 20-25% doctor offices and 9-10% drugs; about 50% of costs are spent on 5% of people.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Hospitals and physician services are the largest pools for disruption.

insights.claim: Driverless cars in some areas are 10-20x safer than human drivers while ~40,000 Americans die yearly in car accidents (similar to breast cancer deaths); the guest says those impeding proven-safe autonomy should have 'a body count attached' and worries healthcare will similarly prioritize jobs over lives.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Regulatory friction, not technology, is the gating factor for AV and AI-in-healthcare adoption.
insights.quote: we cannot prioritize jobs over lives

insights.claim: After raising $500 million at a $5 billion valuation in January 2021, Ro grew only 9% that year and became a 'zombie company' with an ~$800 million preference stack, prompting a 2022 refounding.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Illustrates 2021-vintage valuation overhang risk; turnaround via focus can still yield 10x growth.
insights.quote: you're not growing fast enough to get out of it, but you're not burning where you're going to die

insights.claim: The refounding removed about seven VPs and ~20% of staff, consolidated brands (Roman) under the single Ro brand, codified a 'strong attract, strong repel' culture with explicit 'work hard' principles, and another 6-7% opted out.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Explicit culture resets plus brand consolidation can restore growth at mid-stage companies.

insights.claim: Ro favors sequential over parallel building, ran a daily 8:50am leadership 'steer' meeting for two years, and killed long-term roadmaps as 'false precision' in fast-changing GLP-1 and AI markets.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Operating cadence signals for evaluating execution velocity in fast-moving sectors.
insights.quote: printing out map quests instead of using Google maps

themes.theme: Stigma, celebrities and consumer health marketing

insights.claim: Ro starts with what patients want and finds the overlap with need, avoiding the digital-health graveyard of startups focused on need alone.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Consumer-demand-led health models show stronger adoption than need-led ones.

insights.claim: Stigma signals latent demand: Ro uses celebrity ambassadors who actually use the products (Serena Williams, Charles Barkley, Chrissy Mets, Megan Fox) to create 'permission structures' and shift the Overton window.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Stigmatized categories (weight, ED, reproductive, mental health) offer outsized consumer upside for brands willing to normalize them.

insights.claim: Celebrity faces matter more in the AI era because high-quality ad creative now costs near zero; authentic famous faces cannot be replicated and break through the noise.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Brand moats shift from production quality to authentic, scarce human assets.

insights.claim: The next stigma frontier is prophylactic, early-stage medication use, contrasted with society freely advertising alcohol ('an exchange of poison for entertainment') while resisting drug advertising.
insights.speaker: Ro co-founder/CEO (guest)
insights.so_what: Preventive-medication normalization would expand DTC pharma markets; potential headwind narrative for alcohol.
